Picture this. A homeowner in your town needs a new roof before winter. She grabs her phone, searches in the language she thinks in, and finds two local companies. One has a clear page in Spanish explaining the process, the warranty and how to get a free estimate. The other has a polished website, but every word is in English. Which one do you think gets the call?

If your business serves a local market in the United States and your website only speaks English, you may be losing customers every week without ever knowing they were there.

## The numbers are bigger than most owners think

The U.S. Census Bureau counted 70.1 million Hispanic residents as of July 2025, 21% of the country's population. Sixteen states now have at least a million Hispanic residents, and the list goes well beyond California, Texas and Florida: it includes Georgia, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Washington and Virginia.

Language matters more than ethnicity here. According to the 2024 American Community Survey, 44.9 million people age five and older speak Spanish at home, about one in every seven. Many are fully bilingual: 58.9% say they speak English "very well." That still leaves roughly 18 million people who speak Spanish at home and are not fully comfortable in English.

And they spend. Estimates of Hispanic buying power vary by source, from about $2.8 trillion to more than $4 trillion. Either way, it's one of the largest and fastest-growing consumer markets in the country.

## People buy in the language they trust

CSA Research has been surveying online shoppers for years in its "Can't Read, Won't Buy" series. In its 2020 edition, covering more than 8,700 consumers in 29 countries, 76% said they prefer to buy products with information in their own language, and 40% said they will not buy from websites in other languages at all.

That survey is global, not limited to U.S. Hispanics, but the logic applies at home. The same research has found that consumers are least willing to buy without native-language information when the purchase is expensive or high-stakes, like cars or financial services.

Think about what most local businesses sell: a new roof, a dental implant, a car repair, a legal consultation, an HVAC system. These are exactly the decisions where people want to understand every detail of the quote, the warranty and the fine print before they sign.

There's also the family factor. In many Hispanic households, the person who researches the purchase isn't the only one who decides. A bilingual daughter may find your company, but if her parents can't read your website, she has to translate everything, or she picks the competitor whose page they can all read together.

## What doesn't work

Many businesses try to solve this quickly and end up with something that hurts more than it helps:

**A Google Translate button.** Machine translation of a whole site produces stiff, sometimes wrong Spanish, and search engines usually don't index it as real Spanish content. You won't show up when people search in Spanish.

**One lonely page.** A single "Hablamos Español" page buried in the footer tells visitors you speak Spanish, but gives them nothing to read about your services.

**Spanish from Spain.** Spanish varies a lot by region. A text written for Madrid can sound distant or odd to a family from Mexico, Puerto Rico or Colombia living in Ohio.

**A Spanish site with an English-only phone line.** If the page invites people to call and nobody can help them in Spanish, you lose trust right at the finish line. If you don't have a Spanish speaker on staff, say so honestly and offer a form or text messages instead.

## What works

You don't need to rebuild your whole business. A few focused steps make a real difference:

1. **Create Spanish pages for your main services.** One page per service, written from scratch for your Spanish-speaking customers, not translated word for word.
2. **Answer the questions people actually ask.** A Spanish blog post like "¿Cuánto cuesta cambiar el techo de una casa?" can bring in local searchers your competitors are ignoring.
3. **Update your Google Business Profile.** Add a Spanish description, mention that you serve customers in Spanish, and post updates in both languages.
4. **Ask for reviews in Spanish.** Spanish-speaking customers trust reviews from people like them. When a happy client speaks Spanish, invite them to write the review in Spanish.
5. **Get the technical basics right.** Separate Spanish URLs and hreflang tags help Google show the right version to the right person.

## A quick self-check

Ask yourself these four questions:

If a Spanish-speaking customer lands on my site, can they understand what I do, what it costs and how to contact me?

Do I show up when someone searches for my service in Spanish in my city?

Does my Google Business Profile say anything in Spanish?

When a Spanish speaker calls or writes, does someone answer in a way they understand?

If the answer to most of these is no, there's a real group of customers in your area who can't find you, or can't choose you.
